initial_requirements: Researchers developing high-assurance software need a platform-independent graphical interface for the High Assurance Transformation System. Users should be able to prepare transformation applications, invoke proven transformations on abstract programs, and inspect or manipulate the resulting output without working directly with the underlying command-oriented services. The interface should make experimentation with semantics-preserving program transformation more accessible while retaining confidence in the transformed results.

slots.key: Transformation interruption recovery and retry behavior
slots.value: Prefer recovery from a checkpoint when the underlying transformation service supports it, because some runs are expensive and progress should not be lost unnecessarily. Automatic retry may be used for transient environment failures only if it is clearly safe and does not duplicate work or confuse provenance. If neither recovery nor safe retry is possible, restarting from the beginning is acceptable, but the user must be told exactly what was lost and why. When a recovery or retry does happen, the UI should show a clear before-and-after record of the run, including the checkpoint or failure point, what portion was preserved, what had to be recomputed, whether the resumed execution is still linked to the original run ID or became a new derived run, and any retried or substituted step. The UI should make the lineage very explicit, showing the original execution, each interruption point, and each recovery or retry as a visible chain rather than collapsing them into one status. Researchers ought to be able to tell which output segments were preserved from the first attempt and which came from later recovery steps, ideally with timestamps or step markers. The original run should remain the primary record, but any substantial retry path should also be represented as a derived record so the provenance stays clean and auditable.

topics.topic_content: Inspecting and manipulating transformed output without direct command use

slots.key: Result inspection views for transformed output
slots.value: Inspect or manipulate the resulting output quickly and confidently, with the GUI accurately reflecting transformation results; users need to move from a candidate program to an inspectable result without command-line invocation or service interaction, and the process must reliably support submission, execution, and result inspection because failures or ambiguity at those points interrupt analysis. Deeper inspection is preferred when the program is unusual, the transformation is complex, or the result differs in a surprising way. Extra caution is also needed when a run fails, when the input is large or sensitive, or when validating a transformation intended for reuse in later research. Updates to the interface should preserve researchers' ability to inspect prior results. Researchers should have at least a machine-readable export of the transformed program and, if useful, a shareable view for colleagues reviewing the result; the export format should depend on the state being exported, since intermediate review views may need different output than finalized transformed results, and exports should preserve provenance showing which transformation and inputs produced them. Finalized outputs should definitely be exportable, and review snapshots probably should too, but raw prepare states or half-finished intermediate states should generally not be exported unless explicitly needed for debugging; if an ineligible state is selected for export, the GUI should block it and explain why rather than silently exporting something incomplete or misleading. For resumed runs, the GUI should show subtle but unambiguous provenance markers such as a badge or color-coded status on each output region indicating original, recovered, or retried content; if exported or shared, the marker should carry into metadata and ideally be visible in the file header or record summary so the result is not mistaken for a single uninterrupted execution. Comparison views should let users filter or overlay segments so they can compare only original parts, only retried parts, or the full combined result. The choice between separate, overlaid, or combined comparison views should mainly depend on what the user is trying to inspect and the recovery boundary in the run history: if a retry affected only a particular output region or transformation step, the UI should default to separating that area so provenance is clear, while still allowing an optional combined view for a quick overall check; if the recovery was effectively transparent and did not change semantics or outputs, a combined result view is fine, but the user should still be able to drill down to see the split. The export should carry the run identifier, parent or source run reference, recovery or retry markers, timestamps, the transformation version or service version, a clear record of which outputs were original versus recovered or rerun, and enough context to tie the export back to the exact transformation configuration and any checkpoints used; purely local UI details like temporary layout state may be omitted, but anything affecting traceability or reproducibility should stay in the export.

slots.value: Researchers need to keep track of the transformation settings or parameters they used so they can reproduce or compare runs later; captured settings should include the chosen transformation, any options or flags, the input program reference, and any proof or validation preferences the system uses. The reusable copy should be versioned so its evolution can be tracked and linked back to the approved run or source run for traceability. slots.key: Visibility of provenance in shared review views
slots.value: Users should be able to see a clear before-and-after record of a resumed run, including the checkpoint or failure point, what portion was preserved, what had to be recomputed after recovery, and whether any step was retried or substituted; this should not be hidden behind a single 'completed' status. For comparisons, the interface should let the user filter or overlay segments so they can compare only the original parts, only the retried parts, or the full combined result. The default comparison behavior should depend on what the user is trying to inspect and the recovery boundary in the run history: if the retry affected only a particular output region or transformation step, the UI should separate that area by default for clear provenance while still allowing an optional combined view for a quick overall check; if the recovery was transparent and did not change semantics or outputs, a combined result view is fine, with drill-down available to inspect the split. Comparisons should preserve backward compatibility as much as possible, and if needed, show a clear notice that older records were produced under a previous lineage scheme.

slots.key: Conditions under which a proven transformation may be selected

topics.topic_content: Availability and reliability expectations for research use

slots.key: Required service availability during research sessions
slots.value: Core capabilities need to be reliably available at submission, execution, and result inspection, because those are the points where a failure or ambiguity would interrupt analysis. Researchers also want to move from a candidate program to an inspectable result quickly, without spending time on command-line invocation or service interaction. For repeated transformations, speed matters more during normal exploratory runs when output looks consistent, but deeper inspection is needed if the program is unusual, the transformation is complex, or the result is surprising. Extra caution is also needed when a run fails, when input is large or sensitive, or when validating a transformation intended for later reuse in research. Submission issues should be caught up front with a helpful message before anything runs, transformation failures should be reported as system or service errors during execution, and problems with the resulting program should be shown as result-quality or validation issues after completion so researchers can tell whether to fix input, retry the service, or inspect the output more closely.

topics.topic_content: Confidence in transformed results and protection of sensitive research artifacts

slots.key: Verification information needed to trust transformed results
slots.value: Users should be able to prepare inputs, run proven transformations, and inspect the results in the GUI; success also means the GUI accurately reflects the transformation results so users can trust what they see. Deeper inspection is especially needed when the program is unusual, the transformation is complex, the result is surprising, or a run fails; speed matters more for normal exploratory runs with consistent output. Users are trying to preserve the semantics of the original program and judge whether the transformed result is trustworthy for further analysis or reuse. If sharing, templates, search, audit trails, or collaboration are required for traceability or confidence in the transformed results, that specific piece should be pulled into scope for the first release. Anything that could break existing researcher workflows or change the meaning of results should go through coordination first, including major changes to the transformation invocation flow, saved application formats, or how outputs are displayed and interpreted. Submission issues should be caught up front with a helpful message before anything runs; transformation failures should be reported as system or service errors during execution; result problems should be shown as result-quality or validation issues after the transformation completes so researchers know whether to fix input, retry the service, or inspect the output more closely. The current run should keep its exact configuration as the record of what actually happened, while the reusable copy should be a separate editable object, versioned for evolution, and ideally linked back to the approved run or source run for traceability. For exported results, researchers should be able to save the transformed program in a machine-readable form and, when useful, in a shareable review view; the export format should depend on the state being exported, since an intermediate review view may need different output than a finalized transformed result. Exports should also preserve enough provenance to show which transformation and inputs produced them, including the source program version or input file, the exact transformation name and version, the run timestamp, key options or constraints used, and any proof or validity check with whether the output was fully within proven scope or came from a warning path. Additional provenance for exports is partly undecided: versioning and validation status are important, source traceability should be included in principle so exports can get back to the originating input and run, and the exact fields should be marked to be confirmed until underlying service capabilities are verified. A direct link back to the specific source transformation run or state is preferred for exported outputs; if that link is not possible, provenance should at minimum include a unique run identifier. The export should carry the run identifier, parent or source run reference, recovery or retry markers, timestamps, the transformation version or service version, and a clear record of which outputs were original versus recovered or rerun. It should also include enough context to tie the export back to the exact transformation configuration and any checkpoints used, so someone can audit it later without guessing. I’d only omit fields that are purely local UI details, like temporary layout state, but anything that affects traceability or reproducibility should stay with the export. Existing primary runs and their derived retry records should remain immutable once recorded, so their provenance doesn’t shift after the fact. If the transformation system changes in a way that alters how lineage is interpreted, the UI and backend should version that interpretation rather than rewrite historical records, so older exports and audits still point to the meaning that was valid at the time. For comparisons, the system should preserve backward compatibility as much as possible and, if needed, show a clear notice that older records were produced under a previous lineage scheme.

slots.key: Privacy expectations for stored programs, logs, or proof artifacts
slots.value: Extra caution is expected when the input is sensitive, and when users are validating a transformation they plan to reuse in later research. Researchers also need to keep track of transformation settings or parameters so they can reproduce or compare runs later, and intermediate results or proof-related artifacts may matter if exposed by the system. Settings should capture everything needed to reproduce a run, including the chosen transformation, options or flags, the input program reference, and any proof or validation preferences the system uses. Default settings can be inherited for a new run, but researcher changes for one experiment should be clearly marked as overridden so they do not silently affect later runs. Settings that depend on a specific program or transformation instance should be treated as single-run only unless explicitly defined as reusable. The current run’s configuration should remain the exact record of what actually happened, while the reusable copy should be a separate editable, versioned object that is ideally linked back to the approved run or source run for traceability.

slots.key: Deployment form for the GUI
slots.value: Web GUI only for the first release unless there is a strong need for local file workflows that cannot be handled through upload/download, unless researchers must work offline, or unless they need access to local resources that the web app cannot support cleanly. A desktop option is only needed if people genuinely require access to local resources or disconnected work. It could be justified later if the web GUI falls short on offline work, very large local program inputs, tighter integration with local research tools and file systems, or if security or institutional deployment constraints make browser-based workflow less practical. The desktop version should support more direct local file handling and richer integration with analysis tools, but should not diverge in core transformation behavior from the web app.

slots.key: Acceptance criteria for a successful interface
slots.value: Researchers can prepare inputs by loading or entering a program, configure a transformation application, submit it to the existing services, view the result and basic status or error feedback, and compare before-and-after output to judge whether the transformation looks correct. The interface should also accommodate new transformation types, new parameters, and new result views over time while preserving existing workflows and researchers' saved applications and prior-result inspection. The interface should clearly separate submission issues, transformation failures, and result-quality/validation issues so researchers can tell whether to fix their input, retry the service, or inspect the output more closely. If a program is only partly within a proven transformation's scope, the GUI should flag that clearly before the run and not present it as a fully proven transformation; users should either adjust the input or choose a different fully applicable transformation. Any partial application would need very explicit warning and likely a separate mode, and would be treated as an exception. Existing primary runs and their derived retry records should remain immutable once recorded, and if the transformation system changes in a way that alters lineage interpretation, the UI/backend should version that interpretation rather than rewrite historical records, with backward compatibility preserved as much as possible and clear notices for older records produced under a previous lineage scheme. A derived record should be created whenever the recovery path meaningfully changes execution history in a way that matters for audit or reproducibility, including partial recoveries and retries that reuse preserved state; a truly transparent rerun with nothing preserved should be treated as a new run rather than a derived one.
